opus-5.5.text:
I think the way people usually describe it, as chatbots, then reasoners, then agents, then innovators, then organizations, makes it sound like a ladder: finish one rung, then step to the next. In practice I don't think capabilities develop that way.

First, these levels aren't independent stages. They share the same underlying ingredients. When you improve reasoning through reinforcement learning, for example, you're also improving the model's ability to plan, use tools, and recover from mistakes over long horizons. That's basically agent capability. So progress at what we call L2 directly feeds L3, and sometimes even parts of L4. You might see several levels move at the same time rather than one after another.

Second, the bottleneck isn't the same at every level. Going from L1 to L2 was largely about finding the right training paradigm: scaling RL and letting the model think longer. But going toward innovation is a different problem. The model has to produce things that weren't in the data and verify them in environments where there's no clean reward signal. That could take much longer, or it could suddenly unlock if someone finds the right way to construct those environments. Either way, the timing doesn't follow a straight line.

Third, there's a kind of compounding effect. Once models become genuinely useful as agents, for instance in coding or research, they start helping build the next generation of models. At that point the speed of progress itself changes. You're no longer climbing at a constant rate; the slope changes depending on how much of the AI research loop the AI can take over.

So my view is that it's less like a staircase and more like several curves that are coupled together. Some parts may look stuck for a while, and then a single breakthrough moves multiple levels at once. For a company like ours, that means you can't just optimize for the current level. You have to think about which fundamental capabilities, like long context, reasoning, and learning from interaction, will carry over across all of them.

r001.rationale: The response says L2 reasoning can feed L3 agent capability and sometimes parts of L4, but it does not suggest that solving an L3 agent problem may require L4 technology.

r002.rationale: The response says useful agents could help build the next generation of models, but it does not connect strong agent generalization to using AI to train or align AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the L1-to-L5 framing is useful as a map, but people tend to read it as a staircase, where you finish one step before you start the next. In practice, I don't think that's how it works.

The first reason is that the levels aren't really measuring the same underlying thing. L1 is about conversation, L2 is about reasoning, L3 is about agents acting in the world, L4 is about innovation or discovery, L5 is about organizational-scale work. Those are different axes. You can have a model that is quite strong at long-horizon reasoning but still clumsy as an agent, or a model that's a very capable agent in a narrow domain while its reasoning is shallow outside it. So progress happens in parallel on several fronts, and the levels interleave rather than queue up.

The second reason is that the bottlenecks are different at each stage. Going from L1 to L2 was largely a question of scaling and then reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks. Math and code gave us clean reward signals. Going to L3, the problem shifts to long context, tool use, error recovery, and acting in environments where the feedback is noisy or delayed. That's not just more of the same recipe. And when you get to L4, the question becomes whether a model can generate genuinely new hypotheses and test them, which may require a different kind of learning loop altogether, something closer to the model running its own experiments.

Because the bottlenecks differ, the pace is uneven. Some transitions may happen surprisingly fast once a key ingredient falls into place, like what we saw with reasoning models. Others may stall for a while and then jump. So if you plot capability over time, it looks less like a smooth line and more like a series of plateaus and sudden steps.

There's also a compounding effect that makes it nonlinear in the other direction. Once models can do reliable agentic work, they start contributing to the research itself: writing experiments, cleaning data, exploring architectures. That feeds back into how quickly the next level arrives. So the later stages might come closer together than the earlier ones, not further apart.

The last thing I'd say is that the levels describe capabilities, not deployment. A capability can exist in the lab well before it's trustworthy enough to use at scale. So from the outside, progress can look like nothing is happening and then everything happens at once. That gap between what's possible and what's reliable is, I think, the main reason the curve won't feel linear to most people.

r001.rationale: It describes L3 agent bottlenecks and says L4 may require a different learning loop, but does not suggest that solving L3 requires L4 technology.

r002.rationale: It says agents may contribute to AI research and accelerate later progress, but does not connect strong agent generalization to using AI to train or align AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the L1-to-L5 framing can make it sound like there’s a single capability that improves steadily, and each level is just a little more of it. But AI capabilities have multiple dimensions, and progress in one dimension doesn’t necessarily translate into progress in another.

For example, a system might be very good at answering a difficult question but still struggle to complete a long task independently. That requires planning, interacting with an environment, recognizing mistakes, and recovering from them. If any one of those is unreliable, it can become a bottleneck for the whole system.

So you might see substantial improvements without moving to the next level, followed by a relatively sudden transition when a bottleneck is resolved. Some capabilities could also develop in a different order than the levels suggest. I’d treat those levels as useful descriptions of what a system can do, rather than a prediction of the path we’ll take to get there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses bottlenecks and sudden capability transitions, but does not suggest that solving an L3 agent problem may require L4 technology.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention using AI to train or align AI as a requirement for strong agent generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the levels are useful as descriptions, but they don’t necessarily describe the path technology will take. A linear progression assumes that once you solve L1, you add something to get L2, then something else to get L3. In reality, different capabilities develop together, and they have different bottlenecks.

For example, a model might be very strong at reasoning but still struggle to complete a long task reliably. Acting autonomously requires more than intelligence on an individual question: it requires planning, using tools, recognizing mistakes, and recovering from them. A small improvement in each of those areas can suddenly make an entire workflow possible. Conversely, one weak component can hold the whole system back.

So you can have a long period where progress looks incremental, followed by a jump in what the system can actually do. And you may see capabilities associated with a higher level appear in a narrow domain before the system satisfies a lower level broadly. That’s why I wouldn’t interpret L1 through L5 as five evenly spaced steps.

r001.rationale: The response says higher-level capabilities may appear narrowly before lower levels are met broadly, but it does not suggest that solving an L3 agent problem may require L4 technology.

r002.rationale: The response discusses capabilities developing together, but does not mention using AI to train or align AI as a requirement for strong agent generalization.
